title: Pentecost and ordinary time
hook: after Pentecost comes the long green season, when faith gets lived in the ordinary

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascha, and your line: he is risen indeed. Today, Easter's fiftieth day, and then the longest season of all.

Jerusalem again, seven weeks after Easter. The city is full of pilgrims for a Jewish harvest feast, visitors from all over the known world. Acts says: "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place." Jesus's followers, together in a house. Then a sound like a rushing wind fills the place, and something like flames rests on each of them. They pour into the street talking, and the crowd, people from Egypt, Rome, Arabia, Asia, each hears them in their own language. Some are amazed. Others laugh and say they're drunk, at nine in the morning. It's loud, bright and red. Then the church calendar does something surprising: it turns green, and goes quiet, for months. Today's word is that long quiet.
screen: `SEVEN WEEKS AFTER EASTER.` → `WIND AND FIRE.` → `EVERY LANGUAGE, THEN GREEN.`

segments.voice: Start with Pentecost, Greek for fiftieth. It was a Jewish feast first, Shavuot, the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, and Jews still keep it. Christians remember it as the day the Holy Spirit came, and many call it the birthday of the church. Churches wear red for the fire. Then comes ordinary time. Ordinary doesn't mean boring. It comes from the Latin for numbered, like ordinal numbers: the Sundays are simply counted, the tenth, the eleventh, the twelfth. Some churches call them the Sundays after Pentecost, or after Trinity. The color is green, the color of things growing. It's the longest season of the year, from late spring through summer and fall, about half the calendar. No big feasts, no fasting. Just the Gospels read in order, week after week, and life lived. That's the point. After the waiting and the birth, the desert, the cross, the empty tomb and the fire, the church year says: now go and live it on a Tuesday. Paul wrote: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord." In the 1600s, a Carmelite brother named Lawrence worked in his monastery's kitchen, and said he felt as near to God among the pots and pans as at the altar. So end twelve days on the circle of the year, from Advent's candles to the long green season. The holy days point back to the ordinary ones.
screen: `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `ORDINARY MEANS NUMBERED.` · `GREEN, AND HALF THE YEAR.` · `GOD AMONG THE POTS AND PANS.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary task you'll do today anyway, washing dishes, folding laundry, answering email, and picture yourself doing it slowly, with full attention, as if it mattered. If you pray, offer it to God before you start, as prayer; if you don't, as an act of care for the people it serves.
Ordinary time. The long green season of the church year. Ordinary meaning numbered, not boring: faith lived week by week. Today's word.
Your line: the ordinary is holy. Tomorrow, a new stretch: sabbath and scripture. One hundred twenty days in.

original.note: Greek: the fiftieth day. the feast fifty days after Passover, and after Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: ordinary time means the plain, unimportant weeks.
what it means: the long green season after Pentecost, when faith is lived week by week in everyday life.
what a scholar hears: ordinary from Latin ordinalis, numbered. the name belongs to the Catholic calendar revised in 1969; many Protestant calendars count Sundays after Pentecost or after Trinity.

notes: 'At nine in the morning' follows Acts 2:15 ('the third hour of the day'). Confirm.
Ordinary Time as a named season is from the 1969 Roman calendar; Anglican, Lutheran and other calendars use 'Sundays after Pentecost/Trinity'. Confirm.
Ordinary time also has a short stretch between Epiphany and Lent; the script speaks of the long stretch after Pentecost. Confirm acceptable.
Brother Lawrence (c. 1614–1691), Carmelite lay brother, kitchen work: paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
